summary: Moonova is a strategy-based space astronaut training simulation designed for a young audience, where the narrative unfolds based on the decisions made by the player. The simulation aims to help young people learn about space-related challenges and concepts, while also broadening their general knowledge in this field. Our primary goal is to ensure a successful educational experience without ever compromising on entertainment.
details:
Moonova is a retro pixel-art story game for kids aged 7–12 that runs in any web browser. The player is the youngest astronaut at a colony on the rim of Shackleton crater, at the Moon’s south pole. Together with the crew, the player balances three gauges: ⚡ Power, 💨 Life support (air, water and food) and 🛡 Radiation shield. Those three decide the fourth, the crew’s ❤ Health. A real solar storm is on its way, and it tests every decision the player has made.

How it works. The game has five chapters, and each one teaches one engineering trade-off:

  • Power budget: the antenna needs power, so which system do you turn down?
  • Water = life = shield: the ice found in Shackleton’s permanent shadow can become drinking water, oxygen or radiation shielding. You have to choose.
  • Shield vs. life support: filling the shelter walls with water protects the crew from radiation, but that water can no longer be drunk.
  • Storm prep and the storm itself: four jobs need doing and there is only time for two.

No choice is free. Every option shows its cost, for example “⚡-2 now · 💨-1 later”. Some costs are paid in the next chapter rather than right away, so “power you save today costs oxygen tomorrow” is something players actually feel. Each chapter ends with a Mission Control report that explains in plain language which decision changed which gauge and why, along with the lesson from any mistakes.

In the storm encounter, the player turns a shield ring to deflect particles. How wide the ring is, and how many hits can hurt the crew, depends on the shield the player built up beforehand. That is where preparation pays off. There are four endings, and even the worst one is framed as a lesson rather than a punishment.

Benefits and intended impact. Space education for kids tends to be either too abstract (posters and general facts) or too technical. Moonova turns the decision logic that mission planners deal with into the child’s own choices. We want players to come away understanding that in space everything has a cost, and why.

Tools and technologies. The game is written in plain HTML5 Canvas, JavaScript and CSS, with no frameworks or libraries. Sound effects and the radio “Quindar” beeps are generated in code with the Web Audio API. The landing music is a real NASA recording (Apollo 11 “We Have a Lift-Off”). The background music was generated with Google Gemini (Lyria). Turkish and English text are stored in JSON language files. A PWA manifest and an on-screen touch joystick make it playable on phones. There is nothing to download or install, no account is needed, and it works offline.

Creativity. Instead of a dry dashboard, we built a story with a crew of characters: Nova, the base’s cat-shaped AI; Volt, the robot engineer; Lily, who runs the greenhouse; Dr. Maya, the solar scientist; Captain Leo; and Echo, a small explorer robot found in the crater. Each expert teaches their own field in conversation. Mini-games such as packing a space dinner tray and aligning the antenna turn ideas into hands-on tasks. The game remembers the player’s choices, and the characters bring them up in later chapters.

What our team considered.

  • Not too much at once: only three core gauges, so young players aren’t overwhelmed.
  • Plain language: unavoidable terms such as Kp and µSv are explained where they first appear.
  • Every choice has a cost: there is no “safe” option.
  • Real data: we used sourced NASA data instead of invented numbers.
  • Easy to reach: free, bilingual and runs in a browser.
  • Failure teaches: losing is treated as a lesson, not a punishment.

Data and Sources

All data is a curated archive bundled with the game. Nothing is fetched live, and the game never presents the data as live. Every NASA and partner source below is listed with its link on the in-game Science Notes and Sources screens at the end of the game.

Space weather (Chapters 4–5, storm encounter)

NASA DONKI (Space Weather Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, Information), https://kauai.ccmc.gsfc.nasa.gov/DONKI/

  • Where: the game’s storm record. It covers six X-class flares from 8–11 May 2024 (largest X5.8), two full-halo CMEs, and the 10–13 May 2024 Kp 9 / G5 geomagnetic storm.
  • How it drives play: Dr. Maya’s Chapter 4 warning quotes the storm’s Kp. In Chapter 5, Kp sets the storm’s intensity and number of waves, and the X-class flare makes it harder.
  • Why: DONKI links each flare to its CME and to the storm it caused. That flare → CME → storm chain is exactly the chain the player has to plan around.

NASA CCMC / DONKI Time Period 2024-05-TP-02, https://ccmc.gsfc.nasa.gov/TP/2024-05-TP-02

  • Where: the May 2024 storm record.
  • Why: CCMC’s own summary of this period, which we used to check the flare and CME list.

NASA Science, “How NASA Tracked the Most Intense Solar Storm in Decades”, https://science.nasa.gov/science-research/heliophysics/how-nasa-tracked-the-most-intense-solar-storm-in-decades

  • Where: the May 2024 storm record and the endgame Science Notes.
  • Why: NASA’s own account of the same event, used to confirm it was a G5 storm.

NASA Solar Cycle 25 blog (May 2024), https://blogs.nasa.gov/solarcycle25/2024/05/

  • Where: the May 2024 storm record.
  • Why: a day-by-day check of the flare classes and peak times.

NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center (partner agency), https://www.spaceweather.gov/

  • Where: Dr. Maya’s explanation of flare classes (B, C, M, X) and the Kp scale, plus the endgame Science Notes.
  • Why: NOAA’s R/S/G scales are the official way storms are rated, and Artemis flight controllers use SWPC forecasts. We also used it to cross-check the DONKI values.

STCE Newsletter (Royal Observatory of Belgium), https://www.stce.be/newsletter/

  • Where: background research only; not shown in the game.
  • Why: a third source to check flare begin, peak and end times.

Radiation and the 🛡 Shield gauge (Chapters 4–5)

NASA OCHMO Technical Brief: Radiation Protection (NASA-STD-3001), https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/ochmo-tb-020-radiation-protection.pdf

  • Where: the Shield gauge, the “fill the water walls” storm-prep job, and the Science Notes.
  • Why: it is the source for the 600 mSv career dose limit, for water and hydrogen-rich materials being the best shields, and for storm shelters. That makes “🛡+3, 💨−2: water in the walls is water you can’t drink” a real NASA trade-off.

NASA, “To Protect Artemis II Astronauts, NASA Experts Keep Eyes on Sun”, https://science.nasa.gov/missions/artemis/artemis-2/to-protect-artemis-ii-astronauts-nasa-experts-keep-eyes-on-sun/

  • Where: the Chapter 4 storm-prep story: Dr. Maya watches the Sun and the crew builds a shelter.
  • Why: it describes how NASA watches space weather for a crewed Moon mission and how the Orion crew builds a shelter during a solar event. That is the situation the player is in.

NASA, “How NASA Will Protect Astronauts From Space Radiation at the Moon”, https://science.nasa.gov/science-research/heliophysics/how-nasa-will-protect-astronauts-from-space-radiation-at-the-moon/

  • Where: Dr. Maya’s lessons about solar storms and shelters.
  • Why: it explains how Artemis missions decide when the crew should take shelter, which is the decision the player makes.

Space radiation measurements during Artemis I (Nature, 2024), https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07927-7

  • Where: the Science Notes and the shelter lesson.
  • Why: on Artemis I, the best-protected spot in Orion received far less dose than the least-protected one. That is real evidence that how you build the shelter matters.

NASA OSDR RadLab (ISS dosimeter data), https://visualization.osdr.nasa.gov/radlab/

  • Where: the Chapter 4 meeting. Dr. Maya explains dose rate in µSv per hour, compares Earth, the ISS and the Moon, and asks a quiz based on RadLab’s per-module readings: is it safer to shelter in the glass Cupola or in a thick-walled module? After the storm she saves her dosimeter log “hour by hour, like RadLab”.
  • Why: it ties the Shield gauge to real measured dose. Thicker walls, water and equipment really do mean a lower dose.

Zhang et al., Science Advances 2020 (Chang’e-4 lunar surface dose), https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aaz1334

  • Where: Dr. Maya’s dose comparison (about 57 µSv/hour on the lunar surface).
  • Why: it is the only direct measurement of radiation on the lunar surface. Inside the game it is clearly labelled as Chinese–German, not a NASA measurement.

Site, sunlight, power and water ice (Chapters 1–3, colony map)

NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO), https://science.nasa.gov/mission/lro/

  • Where: the colony map and Volt’s lesson about sunlight at the pole.
  • Why: LRO’s maps of light, temperature and terrain are the basis for where things sit on the colony map.

LOLA Illumination at the Lunar South Pole (Mazarico et al., NASA NTRS), https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20120010094

  • Where: the colony map (the Solar Field sits on the sunlit “Light Ridge”) and Chapter 2, where a ridge’s shadow cuts the Solar Field’s power.
  • Why: it shows that sunlight at the pole depends on the terrain and comes and goes over time. That is the root of the game’s power-budget lesson.

NASA Science, “Shackleton Crater’s Illuminated Rim, Shadowed Interior”, https://science.nasa.gov/resource/shackleton-craters-illuminated-rim-shadowed-interior/

  • Where: the map layout (a bright rim with dark crater floors, the Shackleton ramp) and the crater scene.
  • Why: it is why the base sits on the rim while the ice and Echo are down in the dark.

NASA, “The Lunar South Pole Region”, https://www.nasa.gov/reference/moonbase-environment/

  • Where: Volt’s lesson about the Sun circling just above the horizon, and the cold of the shadowed floors.
  • Why: it describes the environment the colony actually has to deal with.

NASA SSERVI: Shackleton Crater Characterization, https://lunarscience.nasa.gov/articles/detailed-characterization-of-shackleton-crater/

  • Where: the Science Notes and the crater scene.
  • Why: LRO laser data hint at ice on Shackleton’s own floor, which is the crater the player goes down into.

NASA LCROSS (2009), https://science.nasa.gov/mission/lcross/

  • Where: the ice discovery in Chapter 3, when Echo reports about 5.6% water in the dust thrown up from Cabeus crater.
  • Why: it is real evidence of water ice in polar shadows, which makes the Chapter 3 choice (haul the ice or only take a sample) believable.

NASA JPL, “Ice Confirmed at the Moon’s Poles” (M3, 2018), https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/ice-confirmed-at-the-moons-poles/

  • Where: the Chapter 3 ice lesson and the Science Notes.
  • Why: it is the direct confirmation of surface ice in polar shadows.

Life support and food (💨 Life gauge, Chapter 1 and the greenhouse)

NASA ECLSS (ISS Life Support), https://www.nasa.gov/reference/environmental-control-and-life-support-systems-eclss/

  • Where: the Ice Processing Plant (ice → water → oxygen by electrolysis) and its end-of-chapter cost (⚡−1, 💨+1).
  • Why: it is a real, working answer to “how do you make air in space?”, and the answer costs power.

NASA Veggie Fact Sheet, https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/veggie_fact_sheet_508.pdf

  • Where: Lily’s greenhouse lesson (red and blue LED grow lights) and the greenhouse cost (it needs power now and gives oxygen and food later).
  • Why: it grounds the greenhouse trade-off and the delayed payback in a real NASA plant-growth system.

NASA OSDR OSD-268 (VEG-01B lettuce grown on the ISS), https://osdr.nasa.gov/bio/repo/data/studies/OSD-268

  • Where: the greenhouse science note.
  • Why: lettuce grown on the ISS was brought back and compared with lettuce grown on Earth for nutrients and microbes. That is the real research behind “can plants feed a Moon base?”, and it points teachers to where real space-biology data lives.

Canadian Space Agency, “Food Production on the Moon and in Remote Areas” (educator toolkit), https://www.asc-csa.gc.ca/eng/youth-educators/toolkits/food-production/

  • Where: the Chapter 1 “Space Dinner” mini-game. The player sorts seven foods onto a tray, for example a tortilla instead of crumbly bread and liquid salt instead of loose grains. Afterwards the crew explains daily calories (1,900–3,200 kcal), meal routines, why there is no food fridge, taste changes in low gravity, and why calcium and vitamin D matter for bones.
  • Why: it turns the food part of the Life gauge into something kids can do with their hands and remember.

Communication delay (Chapters 1 and 4)

NASA Moon Facts, https://science.nasa.gov/moon/facts/

  • Where: Captain Leo’s lesson. A radio message reaches Earth in about 1.3 seconds, and a reply comes back in about 2.6 seconds.
  • Why: the Earth–Moon distance gives a real, computable delay.

NASA Humans to Mars, https://www.nasa.gov/humans-in-space/humans-to-mars/

  • Where: Leo’s Chapter 4 line, “on Mars we’d wait many minutes for an answer; there the crew has to decide”, which is why the player makes the storm decisions.
  • Why: it shows kids why crews far from Earth need to be able to decide for themselves.

NASA TM-2025 (communication delays), https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20250003885/downloads/NASA%20TM20250003885.pdf

  • Where: the same line from Leo and the Science Notes (Mars is 3–22 minutes away one way).
  • Why: it is NASA’s technical source for the Mars delay range.

Audio

NASA Historical Sounds: Apollo 11 “We Have a Lift-Off”, https://www.nasa.gov/historical-sounds/

  • Where: the music in the landing scene and the finale. It is credited on the in-game Sources screen.
  • Why: the real Apollo 11 countdown, with its Quindar tones, connects the player’s own Moon landing to the first crewed one. It is used under NASA’s media usage guidelines and does not imply endorsement.

Google Gemini (Lyria music model), https://deepmind.google/models/lyria/

  • Where: the three background music tracks: the menu, the main gameplay and the storm encounter.
  • Why: it gave our small team original music that fits each mood without using copyrighted tracks. The music is AI-generated, and we say so here and in the AI use section.
